claim: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-β and misfolded tau proteins causing synaptic dysfunction, and progressive neurodegeneration and cognitive decline.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-β and misfolded tau proteins causing synaptic dysfunction, and progressive neurodegeneration and cognitive decline.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AD pathophysiology, supported by extensive research literature.

claim: Altered neural oscillations have been consistently demonstrated in AD.
source: Altered neural oscillations have been consistently demonstrated in AD.
evidence: This statement references established findings in the field, implicitly drawing on prior research.

claim: Increases in neural synchrony in the delta-theta band showed progressive changes throughout the stages of the EBM.
source: The increases in neural synchrony in the delta-theta band and the decreases in the alpha and beta bands showed progressive changes throughout the stages of the EBM.
evidence: This claim is supported by the EBM analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Decreases in neural synchrony in the alpha and beta bands showed progressive changes throughout the stages of the EBM.
source: The increases in neural synchrony in the delta-theta band and the decreases in the alpha and beta bands showed progressive changes throughout the stages of the EBM.
evidence: This claim is supported by the EBM analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Decreases in alpha and beta band synchrony preceded both neurodegeneration and cognitive decline.
source: Decreases in alpha and beta band synchrony preceded both neurodegeneration and cognitive decline, indicating that frequency-specific neuronal synchrony abnormalities are early manifestations of AD pathophysiology.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the SAC-EBM analyses showing temporal ordering of events.

claim: Frequency-specific neuronal synchrony abnormalities are early manifestations of AD pathophysiology.
source: Decreases in alpha and beta band synchrony preceded both neurodegeneration and cognitive decline, indicating that frequency-specific neuronal synchrony abnormalities are early manifestations of AD pathophysiology.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal ordering observed in the EBM results.

claim: The long-range synchrony effects were greater than the local synchrony.
source: The long-range synchrony effects were greater than the local synchrony, indicating a greater sensitivity of connectivity metrics involving multiple regions of the brain.
evidence: This is based on comparison of AEC and spectral power trajectories in the EBM analyses.

claim: Long-range synchrony metrics have greater sensitivity than local synchrony metrics for detecting connectivity changes involving multiple regions of the brain.
source: The long-range synchrony effects were greater than the local synchrony, indicating a greater sensitivity of connectivity metrics involving multiple regions of the brain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparative magnitude of changes observed in the data.

claim: Aβ accumulation occurs early in the timeline of neuropathological changes in AD, likely preceding the accumulation of tau, and subsequent neurodegeneration and cognitive decline.
source: Clinical and epidemiological studies have suggested that Aβ accumulation occurs early in the timeline of neuropathological changes in AD, likely preceding the accumulation of tau, and subsequent neurodegeneration and cognitive decline (Jack et al., 2010; Sperling et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: The neuropathological changes of AD are described as a continuum, starting from the presymptomatic stage of proteinopathy and continuing to progress during the symptomatic stage with increasing stages of disease severity.
source: The neuropathological changes of AD are, therefore, described as a continuum, starting from the presymptomatic stage of proteinopathy and continuing to progress during the symptomatic stage with increasing stages of disease severity (Sperling et al., 2011; Jack et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conceptual framework supported by cited literature.

claim: AD proteinopathy of Aβ and tau is associated with synaptic and circuit dysfunctions in neural networks in transgenic mouse models.
source: Transgenic mouse models of AD have shown that AD proteinopathy of Aβ and tau is associated with synaptic and circuit dysfunctions in neural networks (Busche et al., 2008; Ahnaou et al., 2017; Busche et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal model studies.

claim: The temporal change in synaptic and circuit dysfunction during disease progression in patients with AD remains largely unknown.
source: However, the temporal change in synaptic and circuit dysfunction during disease progression in patients with AD remains largely unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Abnormal neural oscillation synchrony has been reported in patients along the clinical spectrum of AD, including mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to AD and AD-dementia.
source: In fact, abnormal neural oscillation synchrony has been reported not only in patients along the clinical spectrum of AD, including mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to AD and AD-dementia (Jeong, 2004; Fernández et al., 2006; Stam et al., 2006; Koelewijn et al., 2017; Nakamura et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2019; Ranasinghe et al., 2020; Meghdadi et al., 2021; Schoonhoven et al., 2022) but also during the preclinical stages of AD (Nakamura et al., 2018; Ranasinghe et al., 2022a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Abnormal neural oscillation synchrony has been reported during the preclinical stages of AD.
source: In fact, abnormal neural oscillation synchrony has been reported not only in patients along the clinical spectrum of AD, including mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to AD and AD-dementia (Jeong, 2004; Fernández et al., 2006; Stam et al., 2006; Koelewijn et al., 2017; Nakamura et al., 2018; Hughes et al., 2019; Ranasinghe et al., 2020; Meghdadi et al., 2021; Schoonhoven et al., 2022) but also during the preclinical stages of AD (Nakamura et al., 2018; Ranasinghe et al., 2022a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neuronal oscillations observed by noninvasive electrophysiological measures represent the synchronized activity of excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Neuronal oscillations observed by noninvasive electrophysiological measures, such as electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG), represent the synchronized activity of excitatory and inhibitory neurons and thus provide sensitive indices of altered neuronal and circuit functions in AD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the neurophysiological basis of EEG/MEG signals.

claim: Neuronal oscillations provide sensitive indices of altered neuronal and circuit functions in AD.
source: Neuronal oscillations observed by noninvasive electrophysiological measures, such as electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG), represent the synchronized activity of excitatory and inhibitory neurons and thus provide sensitive indices of altered neuronal and circuit functions in AD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between oscillations and neural function.

claim: Synaptic dysfunction is strongly associated with AD proteinopathy.
source: As synaptic dysfunction is strongly associated with AD proteinopathy, altered neural oscillation synchrony may capture early functional deficits of neural networks even before clinical symptoms appear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD pathophysiology.

claim: Altered neural oscillation synchrony may capture early functional deficits of neural networks even before clinical symptoms appear.
source: As synaptic dysfunction is strongly associated with AD proteinopathy, altered neural oscillation synchrony may capture early functional deficits of neural networks even before clinical symptoms appear.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the relationship between synaptic dysfunction and oscillations.

claim: Event-based sequencing models (EBM) have been successfully used to predict AD progression from cross-sectional biomarker data.
source: To examine the temporal relationship amongst altered neural synchrony, neurodegeneration, and cognitive deficits, we used data-driven disease progression models, specifically event-based sequencing models (EBM), which have been successfully used to predict AD progression from cross-sectional biomarker data (Fonteijn et al., 2012; Young et al., 2014; Young et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior EBM studies.

claim: In an EBM, disease progression is described as a series of discrete events defined as the occurrence of a particular biomarker reaching a threshold abnormal value.
source: In an EBM, disease progression is described as a series of discrete events defined as the occurrence of a particular biomarker reaching a threshold abnormal value, and the estimated likelihood of the temporal sequence of events defines disease progression.
evidence: This describes the methodological framework of EBM.

claim: The study developed a robust EBM framework that is less sensitive to the thresholds for the determination of abnormality.
source: Modifying conventional EBMs to find neurophysiological trajectories, we developed a robust EBM framework that is less sensitive to the thresholds for the determination of abnormality thereby resulting in an unbiased estimation of disease stage probability for each study participant.
evidence: This describes a methodological innovation introduced in this study.

claim: AEC and spectral power are highly reliable MEG resting-state metrics according to test-retest studies.
source: Recent test-retest studies of MEG resting-state metrics have revealed that both metrics are highly reliable (Colclough et al., 2016; Wiesman et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to reliability studies.

claim: The study included 78 patients who met National Institute of Aging–Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) criteria.
source: The present study included 78 patients who met National Institute of Aging–Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) criteria (McKhann et al., 2011; Albert et al., 2011; Jack et al., 2018) and 70 cognitively-unimpaired older adults.
evidence: This describes the study cohort composition.

claim: The study included 70 cognitively-unimpaired older adults.
source: The present study included 78 patients who met National Institute of Aging–Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) criteria (McKhann et al., 2011; Albert et al., 2011; Jack et al., 2018) and 70 cognitively-unimpaired older adults.
evidence: This describes the study cohort composition.

claim: Among 78 AD patients, 20 had autopsy-confirmed AD neuropathology.
source: Among 78 AD patients, 20 had autopsy-confirmed AD neuropathology, other 41 patients were positive on the Aβ-PET scans, plus another nine patients showed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) assays of amyloid and tau levels consistent with AD diagnosis.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic confirmation methods for the patient cohort.

claim: 41 AD patients were positive on the Aβ-PET scans.
source: Among 78 AD patients, 20 had autopsy-confirmed AD neuropathology, other 41 patients were positive on the Aβ-PET scans, plus another nine patients showed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) assays of amyloid and tau levels consistent with AD diagnosis.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic confirmation methods for the patient cohort.

claim: Nine AD patients showed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) assays of amyloid and tau levels consistent with AD diagnosis.
source: Among 78 AD patients, 20 had autopsy-confirmed AD neuropathology, other 41 patients were positive on the Aβ-PET scans, plus another nine patients showed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) assays of amyloid and tau levels consistent with AD diagnosis.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic confirmation methods for the patient cohort.

claim: Eight AD patients were clinically diagnosed based on clinical evaluations and the characteristic pattern of cortical atrophy on MRI.
source: The remaining eight patients were clinically diagnosed, based on clinical evaluations and the characteristic pattern of cortical atrophy on MRI.
evidence: This describes the diagnostic methods for a subset of patients.

claim: Forty-seven control participants were evaluated with Aβ-PET and 8 were read as positive.
source: Forty-seven (out of 70) controls were evaluated with Aβ-PET and 8 were read as positive (39 as negative).
evidence: This describes the amyloid status of the control cohort.

claim: The average age at the time of MEG was slightly higher in the control group than patients with AD.
source: The average age at the time of MEG was slightly higher in the control group than patients with AD (controls, mean ± SE: 70.5±0.99, range: 49.5–87.7; AD, mean ± SE: 63.9±1.01, range: 49.0–84.4) [unpaired t-test: t(146)=−4.708;p<0.001].
evidence: This is a statistical finding from demographic analysis.

claim: The mean MMSE in patients with AD was 22.7±0.43.
source: The mean MMSE in patients with AD was 22.7±0.43 (mean ± SE) while the mean MMSE in the controls 29.2±0.48.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study cohort.

claim: The mean MMSE in controls was 29.2±0.48.
source: The mean MMSE in patients with AD was 22.7±0.43 (mean ± SE) while the mean MMSE in the controls 29.2±0.48.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the study cohort.

claim: GM volumes in the temporal regions are significantly smaller in AD patients than in controls.
source: Group comparisons of GM volumes for each of the anatomical regions included in the AAL3 atlas showed that GM volumes in the temporal regions are significantly smaller in AD patients than in controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from group comparison analysis, supported by figure and supplementary data.

claim: MRI-based studies have reported that MTL volume decreases, especially in the perirhinal and entorhinal cortices, in the early stages of typical AD.
source: The PHG includes the perirhinal and entorhinal cortices of the medial temporal lobe (MTL), and MRI-based studies have reported that MTL volume decreases, especially in the perirhinal and entorhinal cortices, in the early stages of typical AD (Teipel et al., 2006; Echávarri et al., 2011; Matsuda, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior MRI studies.

claim: Increases in delta-theta-band synchrony in patients with AD were identified in frontal regions.
source: For regional long-range synchrony (AEC), increases in delta-theta-band synchrony in patients with AD were identified in frontal regions, and reductions in alpha- and beta-band synchrony were identified in the whole brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, E; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from regional group comparison analysis.

claim: Reductions in alpha- and beta-band long-range synchrony were identified in the whole brain in AD patients.
source: For regional long-range synchrony (AEC), increases in delta-theta-band synchrony in patients with AD were identified in frontal regions, and reductions in alpha- and beta-band synchrony were identified in the whole brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, E; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from regional group comparison analysis.

claim: Increases in delta-theta-band local synchrony (spectral power) in patients with AD were identified in the whole brain.
source: For regional local synchrony (spectral power), increases in delta-theta-band power in patients with AD were identified in the whole brain, and reductions in alpha- and beta-band power were identified in temporal regions and the whole brain, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, F; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a finding from regional group comparison analysis.

claim: Reductions in alpha-band local synchrony were identified in temporal regions in AD patients.
source: For regional local synchrony (spectral power), increases in delta-theta-band power in patients with AD were identified in the whole brain, and reductions in alpha- and beta-band power were identified in temporal regions and the whole brain, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, F; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a finding from regional group comparison analysis.

claim: Reductions in beta-band local synchrony were identified in the whole brain in AD patients.
source: For regional local synchrony (spectral power), increases in delta-theta-band power in patients with AD were identified in the whole brain, and reductions in alpha- and beta-band power were identified in temporal regions and the whole brain, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, F; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a finding from regional group comparison analysis.

claim: The trajectory of PHG volume loss preceded that of MMSE decline.
source: The trajectory of PHG volume loss preceded that of MMSE decline (Figure 1F), consistent with the relationship between brain atrophy and cognitive decline described in a hypothetical model of biomarker trajectories (Jack et al., 2010; Sperling et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from the AC-EBM analysis, supported by figure and consistent with prior models.

claim: Stage 4 of the AC-EBM corresponds to MCI stage.
source: Stage 4, therefore, corresponds to MCI stage, whereas stages 3 and 5 correspond to preclinical-AD and mild AD-dementia stages, respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the PHG z-score range, MMSE score range, and CDR distribution at stage 4.

claim: Stages 3 and 5 of the AC-EBM correspond to preclinical-AD and mild AD-dementia stages, respectively.
source: Stage 4, therefore, corresponds to MCI stage, whereas stages 3 and 5 correspond to preclinical-AD and mild AD-dementia stages, respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the progression pattern and clinical characteristics.

claim: Prominent atrophy with z>1 is observed in the temporal regions starting at stage 4 of the AC-EBM.
source: The GM volume z-scores as a function of the seven stages showed that prominent atrophy with z>1 is observed in the temporal regions starting at stage 4 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from the trajectory analysis shown in the figure.

claim: GM volume loss in AD starts in the MTL in the MCI stage, spreads to the lateral temporal and parietal lobes in the mild AD-dementia stage, and spreads further to the frontal lobe in moderate AD-dementia.
source: This trajectory of GM volume approximated the evolution of brain atrophy in the typical progression of AD reported in MRI-based studies; GM volume loss in AD starts in the MTL in the MCI stage, spreads to the lateral temporal and parietal lobes in the mild AD-dementia stage, and spreads further to the frontal lobe in moderate AD-dementia (Scahill et al., 2002; Tondelli et al., 2012; Jack et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior MRI studies and is consistent with the current study's findings.

claim: The delta-theta-band synchrony was consistently increased along the EBM stages.
source: Along the EBM stages, the delta-theta-band synchrony was consistently increased and the alpha and beta-band synchrony was consistently decreased.
evidence: This is a finding from the neural synchrony profile analysis along AC-EBM stages.

claim: The alpha and beta-band synchrony was consistently decreased along the EBM stages.
source: Along the EBM stages, the delta-theta-band synchrony was consistently increased and the alpha and beta-band synchrony was consistently decreased.
evidence: This is a finding from the neural synchrony profile analysis along AC-EBM stages.

claim: Neural synchrony showed prominent changes around stage 4 (clinical stage of MCI due to AD).
source: Neural synchrony showed prominent changes around stage 4 (clinical stage of MCI due to AD).
evidence: This is an observation from the trajectory analysis.

claim: Long-range synchrony in the alpha and beta bands decreased steadily in stages 1–3 and then decreased further in stage 4.
source: The long-range synchrony in the alpha and beta bands decreased steadily in stages 1–3 and then decreased further in stage 4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the trajectory analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Local synchrony in the beta band decreased by half from stage 1 to 4.
source: Local synchrony in the beta band also decreased by half from 1 to 4 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the trajectory analysis.

claim: Long-range synchrony in the alpha and beta bands decreased markedly during the preclinical stages of AD, preceding both PHG volume loss and MMSE decline.
source: Long-range synchrony in the alpha and beta bands decreased markedly during the preclinical stages of AD, preceding both PHG volume loss and MMSE decline.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the SAC-EBM analysis.

claim: Between stages 1 and 4, the alpha- and beta-band long-range synchrony decreased by more than 80% of the total drop seen from stage 1 to 10.
source: Specifically, between stages 1 and 4, the alpha- and beta-band long-range synchrony decreased by more than 80% of the total drop seen from stage 1 to 10.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the SAC-EBM trajectory analysis.

claim: The whole brain, but especially the temporal area, was involved in prominent preclinical changes in alpha and beta long-range synchrony.
source: The whole brain, but especially the temporal area, was involved in these prominent preclinical changes (Figure 3H and L).
evidence: This is a finding from the regional analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The trajectory of delta-theta-band long-range synchrony was almost identical to the evolution of the PHG volume loss throughout the stages.
source: In contrast, the trajectory of delta-theta-band long-range synchrony (Figure 3B and C) was almost identical to the evolution of the PHG volume loss throughout the stages, but a large variation occurred around the MCI stages (stages 5 and 6) as was found in the AC-EBM (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the SAC-EBM analysis.

claim: There were no significant increases in region-level delta-theta band synchrony during the preclinical stages.
source: There were no significant increases in region-level synchrony in delta-theta band during the preclinical stages (Figure 3D), consistent with an observation seen in the AC-EBM (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the regional comparison analysis.

claim: Local synchrony in the alpha and beta bands decreased during the preclinical stages of AD, preceding both PHG volume loss and MMSE decline.
source: Local synchrony in the alpha and beta bands decreased during the preclinical stages of AD, preceding both PHG volume loss and MMSE decline (Figure 4F and G and Figure 4J and K).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the SAC-EBM analysis with local synchrony metrics.

claim: The local synchrony in the delta-theta band increased, lagging the evolution of PHG volume loss.
source: On the contrary, the local synchrony in the delta-theta band increased, lagging the evolution of PHG volume loss (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the SAC-EBM analysis with local synchrony metrics.

claim: The alpha-band local synchrony decreased considerably by the onset of the MCI stage, showing significant reductions in the temporal regions during the preclinical stages.
source: Specifically, the alpha-band local synchrony decreased considerably by the onset of the MCI stage, showing significant reductions in the temporal regions (Figure 4H) during the preclinical stages (stages 6 vs 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the trajectory and regional analysis.

claim: By stage 5, the beta-band power decreased by approximately 55% of the total drop seen throughout the stages.
source: Beta-band local synchrony also decreased during the preclinical stages, preceding PHG volume loss and MMSE decline; by stage 5, the beta-band power decreased by approximately 55% of the total drop seen throughout the stages, and the reductions were observed in the whole brain (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the trajectory analysis.

claim: The decreases in the long-range metrics were much greater than those in the local metrics, especially in the early stages during the phase of preclinical AD (stages 1–3).
source: Notably, the decreases in the long-range metrics were much greater than those in the local metrics, especially in the early stages during the phase of preclinical AD (stages 1–3).
evidence: This is a comparative finding between long-range and local synchrony trajectories.

claim: Functional deficits of frequency-specific neural synchrony show progressive changes across AD stages.
source: We demonstrated that functional deficits of frequency-specific neural synchrony show progressive changes across AD stages.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Both long-range and local neural synchrony in the alpha and beta bands, but not in the delta-theta band, was found to decrease in preclinical stages of AD, preceding neurodegeneration and cognitive decline.
source: Both long-range and local neural synchrony in the alpha and beta bands, but not in the delta-theta band, was found to decrease in preclinical stages of AD, preceding neurodegeneration and cognitive decline, with more robust findings for long-range neural synchrony.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: The findings for long-range neural synchrony were more robust than for local neural synchrony.
source: Both long-range and local neural synchrony in the alpha and beta bands, but not in the delta-theta band, was found to decrease in preclinical stages of AD, preceding neurodegeneration and cognitive decline, with more robust findings for long-range neural synchrony.
evidence: This is a comparative assessment of the findings.

claim: Synchrony reductions in the alpha and beta bands are sensitive indices reflecting functional deficits in the earliest stages of disease progression.
source: These findings highlight the frequency-specific manifestations of neural synchrony in AD and that synchrony reductions in the alpha and beta bands are sensitive indices reflecting functional deficits in the earliest stages of disease progression.
evidence: This is an interpretation and conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: Functional deficits as depicted by reduced neural synchrony precede structural volume loss and cognitive deficits.
source: A key finding of the current study is that functional deficits as depicted by reduced neural synchrony precede structural volume loss and cognitive deficits.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the EBM analyses.

claim: Alpha- and beta-band synchrony within the inferior temporal and posterior parieto-occipital regions show significant deficits in the early disease stages–stages where volumetric and clinical deficits are still not significantly deviated from their baseline trajectory.
source: The EBMs on cross-sectional data clearly demonstrated that alpha- and beta-band synchrony within the inferior temporal and posterior parieto-occipital regions show significant deficits in the early disease stages–stages where volumetric and clinical deficits are still not significantly deviated from their baseline trajectory.
evidence: This is a finding from the EBM analyses.

claim: Functional changes occur earlier in the time course than structural changes in AD.
source: This is consistent with the finding that functional changes occur earlier in the time course than structural changes in AD (Jack et al., 2010; Sperling et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: Previous functional MRI studies have demonstrated disrupted connectivity especially between the hippocampus and several areas of the cortical default mode network (DMN) in subjects with amyloid deposition but without cognitive impairment.
source: Previous functional MRI studies have demonstrated disrupted connectivity especially between the hippocampus and several areas of the cortical default mode network (DMN) in subjects with amyloid deposition but without cognitive impairment (Sperling et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior fMRI research.

claim: Disruption in DMN has been observed in clinically normal older individuals without prominent brain atrophy in MTL that preserves hippocampal activity.
source: This disruption in DMN has also been observed in clinically normal older individuals without prominent brain atrophy in MTL that preserves hippocampal activity (Miller et al., 2008; Hedden et al., 2009), indicating altered functional connectivity during the preclinical period of AD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Oscillatory deficits and their temporal association with neurodegeneration and cognitive decline are frequency-specific.
source: We demonstrated that oscillatory deficits and their temporal association with neurodegeneration and cognitive decline are frequency-specific.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: Alpha and beta hyposynchrony is more tightly associated with tau accumulation, which is closely allied to neurodegeneration and cognitive decline.
source: This is consistent with previous findings that alpha and beta hyposynchrony is more tightly associated with tau accumulation, which is closely allied to neurodegeneration and cognitive decline (Pusil et al., 2019; Ranasinghe et al., 2020; Ranasinghe et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: Neural hyposynchrony in the alpha and beta bands may represent harbingers of altered synaptic physiology associated with tau accumulation in AD.
source: Neural hyposynchrony in the alpha and beta bands may, therefore, represent harbingers of altered synaptic physiology associated with tau accumulation in AD.
evidence: This is an interpretation and hypothesis based on the findings and prior literature.

claim: In human postmortem studies, the strongest correlate of cognitive deficits in AD patients is loss of synapse.
source: In fact, in human postmortem studies, the strongest correlate of cognitive deficits in AD patients is loss of synapse (DeKosky and Scheff, 1990; Terry et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to postmortem studies.

claim: A study using transgenic AD mice has shown that synaptotoxicity is an early phenomenon in AD pathophysiology.
source: A study using transgenic AD mice has also shown that synaptotoxicity is an early phenomenon in AD pathophysiology (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an animal model study.

claim: Delta-theta oscillatory activity increases in AD and is strongly associated with amyloid accumulation.
source: Previous studies have also shown that delta-theta oscillatory activity increases in AD and is strongly associated with amyloid accumulation (Ranasinghe et al., 2020; Ranasinghe et al., 2022b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Oscillatory changes in the delta-theta band may be more closely related to amyloid accumulations in AD, which become saturated early in the disease course and have a poor association with neurodegeneration and cognitive trajectories.
source: This apparent controversy may be due to the possibility that oscillatory changes in the delta-theta band are more closely related to amyloid accumulations in AD, which become saturated early in the disease course and have a poor association with neurodegeneration and cognitive trajectories.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed trajectory of delta-theta synchrony.

claim: The decrease in alpha and beta-band long-range metrics in the preclinical stages was much greater than that in the local metrics.
source: The decrease in alpha and beta-band long-range metrics in the preclinical stages was much greater than that in the local metrics.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the SAC-EBM analyses.

claim: AD-related abnormal brain activities are observed as disruptions of functional networks.
source: This is consistent with the fact that AD-related abnormal brain activities are observed as disruptions of functional networks.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AD pathophysiology.

claim: Long-range cross-regional metrics directly capture network disruptions involving all brain regions, while local metrics capture features of individual regions.
source: Long-range cross-regional metrics, such as AECs, directly capture network disruptions involving all brain regions, while local metrics capture features of individual regions.
evidence: This is an explanation of the methodological differences between the two types of metrics.

claim: Local synchrony describes collective neuronal oscillations in each local region, and thus the change along AD progression may depend mainly on long-term, slowly changing regional neuronal loss.
source: From the definition, local synchrony describes collective neuronal oscillations in each local region, and thus the change along AD progression may depend mainly on long-term, slowly changing regional neuronal loss.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what local synchrony measures and how it changes.

claim: Long-range synchrony describes temporal coherence amongst regional collective neuronal oscillations and is vulnerable to altered neuronal oscillations.
source: On the other hand, long-range synchrony describes temporal coherence amongst regional collective neuronal oscillations and is vulnerable to altered neuronal oscillations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what long-range synchrony measures and its sensitivity.

claim: Long-range metrics are more sensitive to abnormal rhythms, collecting local abnormalities.
source: Therefore, long-range metrics are more sensitive to abnormal rhythms, collecting local abnormalities.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of long-range and local metrics.

claim: Alpha- and beta-band MEG metrics, especially long-range synchrony metrics (AEC), could be promising candidates as additional preclinical markers for AD.
source: From this point of view, the present study indicates that alpha- and beta-band MEG metrics, especially long-range synchrony metrics (AEC), which were found to be sensitive to preclinical stages, could be promising candidates as additional markers.
evidence: This is a conclusion and suggestion based on the study findings.

claim: There were differences in age between controls and AD patients.
source: A limitation of the current study is that there were differences in age between controls and AD patients.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a study limitation.

claim: Age trajectories in neurophysiological measures have been reported to be nonlinear even in healthy aging.
source: Although we adjusted the age of each metric using GLMs, age trajectories in neurophysiological measures have been reported to be nonlinear even in healthy aging (Sahoo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Age-related changes in brain atrophy have been reported to follow a nonlinear time course depending on the brain areas.
source: Age-related changes in brain atrophy have also been reported to follow a nonlinear time course depending on the brain areas (Coupé et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The study has not performed independent validations of the predicted trajectories.
source: Another limitation is that we have not performed independent validations of the predicted trajectories and also have not examined the heterogeneity in AD progression, although we clarified for the first time the time courses of MEG neurophysiological metrics in AD progression.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a study limitation.

claim: The study has not examined the heterogeneity in AD progression.
source: Another limitation is that we have not performed independent validations of the predicted trajectories and also have not examined the heterogeneity in AD progression, although we clarified for the first time the time courses of MEG neurophysiological metrics in AD progression.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a study limitation.

claim: AD is a heterogeneous multifactorial disorder with various pathobiological subtypes.
source: In fact, AD is a heterogeneous multifactorial disorder with various pathobiological subtypes (Jellinger, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Oscillatory rhythms are thought to depend on AD subtypes.
source: Since oscillatory rhythms are thought to depend on AD subtypes (Ranasinghe et al., 2017; Ranasinghe et al., 2022a), an extended trajectory analysis considering spatial and temporal variations of the MEG/EEG metrics is warranted in the future, and such analyses would provide distinct neurophysiological trajectories depending on AD subtypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.
